rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 <U+2014> the authors run their own ISAREG simulations (daily data 2001-2003 and 10-day data 1970-2003) for cotton at the Azizbek-1 farm, Fergana; model previously calibrated/validated with their own field data (Fig. 1 compares observed and simulated soil water for 2001 and 2003). Q2: Section 2.1 and 3.2-3.3, Tables 7-13 <U+2014> ISAREG uses the FAO56 Kc-ETo approach and the Stewart/Doorenbos-Kassam yield function (Eq. 2) to search full and deficit schedules under water scarcity; results show current schedules percolate ~20% of applied water and that mild deficit schedules save up to ~25% irrigation water with RYL under 11%; simulated soil water agrees with observations (Fig. 1) and simulated yields are in accordance with field-measured yields (Section 3.2.3). Q4: Tables 6-8, 10-12 and Figs. 4-6 <U+2014> the model computes the intermediate water-balance terms (available soil water, deep percolation, groundwater contribution, ETa/ETc) through which scheduling produces water saving and yield effects. Q7: Section 3.2.3 end and Section 3.3.3/Conclusions <U+2014> authors state that water saving strategies imply improved farm irrigation systems able to apply the preferred depths (70 mm), delaying the first irrigation, maximizing use of soil water and groundwater contribution, and improvements in delivery scheduling and furrow irrigation performance. Q8: Section 3.1 and Conclusions <U+2014> authors note that the years with daily data (2001-2003) are low-demand/wet years (2003 the most humid of the series), and in 3.2.3 that simulated WP is slightly higher than field values because larger depths were applied in the field studies.
rows.notes: Evidence is model-based: the improved schedules themselves were not field-tested, but the model output was checked against observed soil water and measured yields at the same site, so Q2 is accepted. Q3 no: simulation is the single method. Q5 no: one farm, one crop; climatic demand scenarios and years are not distinct sites. Q6 no: single experimental farm; GIS version mentioned only in passing. Q8 is weak (limitation on representativeness of the experimental period). Q9 no: ranges of RYL across years/scenarios are not dispersion measures; NIR non-exceedance probabilities characterize input demand, not uncertainty of the result.

notes: Full text appears complete. The passage cites Pereira et al. (2009b) as an example of applying a simulation model with FAO56 methodology to search improved schedules under water scarcity; this study does exactly that for cotton in Fergana.
